decks.title: From the Diary of Anne Frank
goals: Retell the main ideas and events of the diary extract in sequence, in your own words
Explain why Anne valued a diary and her views on friendship and loneliness
Describe Anne's personality and her relationship with Mr Keesing
Identify features of the diary form and the humour in the extract
Answer extract-based, short and long questions within the word limits

slides.heading: From the Diary of Anne Frank
slides.body_md:
*First Flight*, prose · diary (extract) · Class 10 CBSE English.

**Read the chapter itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT).** This lesson is SOYL's explanation and analysis; it does not reproduce the diary.

rows: an extract with short questions (answer A or B)
100–120 words: character, theme, diary, letter or opinion

visual.alt: Table of how a First Flight prose lesson is examined: a five-mark reference to context extract, three-mark short answers of forty to fifty words, and a six-mark long answer of one hundred to one hundred and twenty words.
visual.caption: CBSE 2026-27, Section C (literature).

slides.narration: Welcome. Today we study entries from the diary of Anne Frank, one of the most widely read books in the world. Before anything else, please read the chapter itself in your textbook, First Flight. This lesson does not repeat the diary. Instead we will understand Anne's ideas, her personality, her teacher Mr Keesing, the diary form, and how to answer board questions.

slides.heading: How to use this lesson
bullets: Read the extract once in *First Flight*, straight through.
Then use these slides for the background, ideas, characters and the diary form.
In answers, describe events **in your own words**; do not memorise lines.
Practise the extract questions, which use SOYL commentary on the chapter.
slides.narration: Here is how to study this chapter. Read the extract once in your textbook, straight through. Then use these slides for the background, the main ideas, the characters and the diary form. In your answers, describe events in your own words, because examiners reward understanding, not memorised lines. Finally, practise with our extract questions and short answers.

slides.heading: Who was Anne Frank?

a present for her thirteenth birthday, 12 June 1942; she wrote to an imaginary friend, Kitty
entries from June 1942, written a few weeks before the family went into hiding
published by her father, Otto Frank, in 1947; known in English as *The Diary of a Young Girl*
diary: first person, dated entries, private and informal
her parents, sister Margot, grandmother, Mrs Kuperus, Mr Keesing, friends G.Z. and Sanne

visual.alt: Table of facts: Anne Frank, 1929 to 1945, a Jewish girl born in Frankfurt who grew up in Amsterdam; the diary was a thirteenth birthday present in June 1942, addressed to Kitty; this extract dates from June 1942, before the family hid; it was published by her father Otto Frank in 1947; it is a first-person diary; people named include her family, Mrs Kuperus, Mr Keesing, G.Z. and Sanne.

slides.narration: Anne Frank was a Jewish girl, born in Frankfurt in Germany in nineteen twenty-nine. Her family moved to Amsterdam to escape Nazi persecution. On her thirteenth birthday, in June nineteen forty-two, she was given the notebook that became her diary. Our extract comes from the first weeks of that diary. Her father published it after the war, in nineteen forty-seven.

slides.heading: Background: Anne's life and times
slides.body_md: The extract was written in June 1942, *before* the family went into hiding. Readers know what Anne could not.

visual.alt: Timeline of Anne Frank's life: born in Frankfurt in 1929; family moves to Holland in 1933 and 1934; the diary begins in June 1942; the family goes into hiding in July 1942; arrested in August 1944; she dies in Bergen-Belsen in 1945; the diary is published in 1947.
visual.caption: Historical background (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: This timeline matters. Anne was born in nineteen twenty-nine, and her family moved to Holland to escape persecution. In June nineteen forty-two she began her diary. A few weeks later the family went into hiding in Amsterdam. In August nineteen forty-four they were arrested, and Anne died in a camp in nineteen forty-five. The extract comes before all that sadness.

slides.heading: The extract in six parts
slides.body_md: Three parts about the diary itself, one about her past, two about school. (A SOYL summary, not the text.)

visual.alt: Flow of the extract in six parts: why a diary; no true friend; naming the diary Kitty; a sketch of her life; school and the promotion bets; Mr Keesing's three essays.
visual.caption: The extract in six parts (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: The extract moves in six parts. First, why keep a diary at all. Second, Anne's feeling that she has no true friend. Third, her decision to name the diary Kitty. Fourth, a short sketch of her life. Fifth, school, where the whole class is betting on promotions. And sixth, the funny contest with her maths teacher, Mr Keesing. Keep this map in mind.

slides.heading: Summary 1: why a diary?
slides.body_md: Anne admits that keeping a diary feels strange: she has never written like this, and she suspects nobody will care about a young girl's thoughts. But the urge to write wins, because she has feelings she cannot share aloud. She recalls an old saying comparing the patience of paper with the patience of people, and agrees with it. Since she means to show the diary to no one, it can hold anything.
slides.narration: In your own words, the extract begins with a question: why write a diary? Anne admits it feels strange. She has never written like this, and she doubts anyone will care. But she wants to write, because she has feelings she cannot share aloud. She recalls an old saying about paper being more patient than people, and she agrees. A private diary can hold anything.

slides.heading: Summary 2: no true friend, so Kitty
slides.body_md: Anne lists what she has: loving parents, a sixteen-year-old sister, relatives, a good home and many friends and admirers. But with them she talks only about everyday things, and nobody is close enough to confide in. She even wonders if the fault is partly hers. So she decides that the diary itself will be her friend, and she names it Kitty.
slides.narration: Next comes the heart of the extract. Anne has a loving family, a good home and many friends. But she cannot talk to anyone about anything deeper than everyday things. Nobody is truly close. She even wonders if this is partly her fault. So she decides that the diary will be the friend she lacks, and she names it Kitty.

slides.heading: Summary 3: a sketch of her life
slides.body_md: Because Kitty is a new friend, Anne gives some background. Her parents married when her father was thirty-six and her mother twenty-five. Margot was born in Frankfurt in 1926, Anne in 1929. Being Jewish, her father moved to Holland in 1933 to run the Opekta Company; the girls stayed with their grandmother in Aachen before joining him. Anne went to a Montessori nursery school, and later Mrs Kuperus, the headmistress, taught her. Her grandmother died in January 1942.
slides.narration: Since Kitty is a new friend, Anne gives some background. Margot was born in Frankfurt in nineteen twenty-six, and Anne in nineteen twenty-nine. Because they were Jewish, the family moved to Holland, the girls first staying with their grandmother in Aachen. Anne went to a Montessori school, and parted from her headmistress, Mrs Kuperus, in tears. Her grandmother died in January nineteen forty-two.

slides.heading: Check: Anne's life in order
slides.narration: Your turn. Six events from Anne's sketch of her life are shuffled. Put them in the order in which they happened. Use the dates you have just learnt as your guide.

slides.heading: Summary 4: school and the promotion bets
slides.body_md: At school, the whole class is anxious about the teachers' meeting that will decide who moves up to the next form. Half the class is betting on the outcome. Anne and her friend G.Z. laugh at two boys who have bet all their holiday savings. Anne is fairly confident about herself and her friends; only maths worries her.
slides.narration: Then Anne turns to school news. Everyone is nervous about the meeting where teachers decide who moves up to the next form. Half the class is betting, and Anne and her friend G.Z. find two boys who have bet all their holiday savings very funny. Anne feels quite confident about herself and her friends. Her one worry is maths.

slides.heading: Summary 5: the contest with Mr Keesing
slides.body_md: Mr Keesing, the maths teacher, is annoyed by Anne's talking. Three punishment essays follow; the third is answered with a poem.

nodes.label: Essay 3: a silly title about quacking
He reads it out; no more punishment

visual.alt: Flow of the contest with Mr Keesing: warnings about talking; essay one, A Chatterbox; essay two, An Incorrigible Chatterbox; essay three, a silly title about quacking; a poem written with Sanne; he reads it out and stops the punishments.
visual.caption: Anne versus Mr Keesing (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: The extract ends with a battle of wits. Mr Keesing is fed up with Anne's talking and sets an essay on being a chatterbox. Anne argues that talking runs in her family, and he laughs. She keeps talking, so he sets a second essay, and then a third with a silly title about quacking. With her friend Sanne, Anne answers in verse, and wins him over.

slides.heading: Theme 1: why Anne valued a diary
slides.body_md: The diary gives Anne what people around her do not.
columns:
**What people offered**

- fun and everyday chatter
- company, but not closeness
- listeners who might tire or judge

**What the diary offered**

- complete privacy
- patience: it accepts every mood
- a friend, Kitty, to confide in
slides.narration: Why did Anne value her diary so much? Compare what people offered her with what the diary offered. People gave her fun and company, but not closeness, and they might tire or judge. The diary offered complete privacy and endless patience, and by naming it Kitty, Anne turned it into the friend she lacked. That is the key to the first part of the extract.

slides.heading: Theme 2: friendship and loneliness
slides.body_md: It is possible to be lonely in a crowd.
columns:
**Seen from outside**

- a loving family and a good home
- many friends and admirers
- a lively, popular schoolgirl

**Felt inside**

- no one to share secrets with
- conversations that stay on the surface
- a longing for one true friend
slides.narration: The second theme is friendship and loneliness. From the outside, Anne seems lucky: a loving family, many friends, and a lively, popular personality. Inside, she feels alone, because her conversations stay on the surface and she has no one to share secrets with. Anne shows us that the number of friends matters less than the depth of one friendship.

slides.heading: Check: why the diary became a friend
slides.narration: Try this assertion and reason item. Decide whether each statement is true, and then whether the reason really explains the assertion.

slides.heading: Character: Anne
slides.body_md: Every trait in an answer needs an incident, described in your own words.

rows: Her chatter in maths lessons earns three punishments.
She argues her case and answers the silliest title with a poem.
She feels she has no true friend despite many companions.
She wonders whether the distance is partly her own fault.
She still loves her late grandmother; she parted from Mrs Kuperus in tears.
She expects to move up, unsure only about maths.

visual.alt: Table of Anne's traits with evidence: talkative and lively, witty and intelligent, lonely and reflective, honest and self-aware, affectionate and sensitive, and confident.

slides.narration: Let us sketch Anne. She is talkative and lively, which gets her into trouble. She is witty and intelligent, as her essays and poem show. She is lonely and reflective, and honest enough to ask whether the fault is hers. She is affectionate, remembering her grandmother and Mrs Kuperus with love. And she is confident about school. Back every trait with an incident.

slides.heading: Character: Mr Keesing

rows: He warns Anne repeatedly and sets punishment essays.
Each time she keeps talking, he sets a new essay.
He laughs at her arguments and invents a comic third title.
He enjoys her poem, reads it to several classes and stops the punishments.

visual.alt: Table of Mr Keesing's traits with evidence: strict, persistent, humorous, and fair and open-minded.

slides.narration: Now Mr Keesing. Anne calls him old-fashioned, but he is more than that. He is strict, warning her and setting punishments. He is persistent, setting a new essay each time she keeps talking. He has a sense of humour, laughing at her arguments and inventing a comic title. And he is fair, because when her poem beats him, he enjoys it and stops punishing her.

slides.heading: Check: Mr Keesing's approach today
slides.narration: Check yourself. A student keeps drawing cartoons in class. Which teacher's response is most like Mr Keesing's final approach to Anne? Think about how the contest ended.

slides.heading: The diary form

rows: we hear Anne's own voice and feelings
complete honesty about loneliness and doubt
warm, conversational tone, like a letter to a friend
her life story and the day's school news side by side
a lively schoolgirl's voice, full of humour

visual.alt: Table of features of the diary form and their effects: first person, private, addressed to Kitty, past and present mixed, and informal style, giving honesty, warmth and liveliness.

slides.narration: Now the form. A diary is written in the first person, so we hear Anne's own voice. It is private, so she can be completely honest. Anne adds a twist by addressing Kitty, which makes it warm and conversational, like a letter. She mixes her past with the day's news. And her informal style gives us the voice of a real schoolgirl, full of humour.

slides.heading: Humour in the extract
bullets: **Situation:** two boys bet all their holiday savings on the promotion results.
**Escalation:** each punishment title is sillier than the last.
**Reversal:** the punished pupil wins; the joke ends up on the teacher.
**Self-mockery:** Anne laughs at her own chatter and its supposed family origin.
**Light tone** that contrasts with the dark history readers know.
slides.narration: The extract is genuinely funny. There is comedy of situation, in the two boys who bet all their holiday savings. There is escalation, as each punishment title gets sillier. There is reversal, because the punished pupil wins and the joke ends up on the teacher. Anne laughs at herself too. And this light tone moves us all the more because we know what came later.

slides.heading: Writing a diary entry: SOYL's own model lines
slides.body_md: Board extrapolation tasks often ask for a diary entry. These lines are SOYL's own, showing the features of the form:
bullets: *Tuesday, 14 March, 9 p.m.* — date and time
*Dear Diary, today I finally said sorry to Riya, and the knot in my stomach has gone.* — first person, feelings, a friendly address
*Tomorrow I must remember to return her book.* — a look ahead to end the entry
slides.narration: Board papers often ask you to write a diary entry. Here are some lines of our own showing the features. Start with a date and time. Then write in the first person, with feelings, perhaps addressing the diary as a friend, as Anne does with Kitty. End by looking ahead. Keep header lines short, and write the entry in your own words, never copying the textbook.

slides.heading: Word meanings

rows: thinking deeply about something that makes one unhappy
to share secrets or private feelings with someone
left one country to live in another

visual.alt: Table of word meanings: musings, listless, brooding, confide, emigrated, incorrigible, fogey and ingenuity.
visual.caption: Single words from the chapter with their meanings.

slides.narration: These words from the chapter are worth learning. Musings are quiet thoughts. Listless means without energy. Brooding is thinking unhappily. To confide is to share secrets. Emigrated means moved to another country to live. Incorrigible means impossible to correct. A fogey is an old-fashioned, dull person. And ingenuity is cleverness, which Anne certainly had.

slides.heading: Worked example: planning a 6-mark answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* *Anne was witty as well as thoughtful.* Do you agree?
bullets: **Stand:** agree.
**Points + incidents:** turns punishments into clever arguments; answers the silliest title with a poem; reflects honestly on loneliness and her own part in it.
**Link:** wit and reflection together make the diary's voice real.
**Conclusion:** a lively girl with a deep inner life.

visual.alt: Flow for planning a six-mark long answer: take a stand, give points with incidents in your own words, link to a theme, and conclude.

slides.narration: Here is how to plan a six mark answer. Take a clear stand: agree. Give three points with incidents in your own words: her clever essay arguments, her poem, and her honest reflection on loneliness. Link this to the theme of the diary's honest voice. End with a one-line conclusion. That plan becomes an answer of about one hundred and ten words.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Context: a Jewish girl in Amsterdam, writing in June 1942, weeks before hiding; died 1945; diary published 1947.
Why a diary: no true friend; paper's patience; complete privacy; Kitty.
Life sketch: Frankfurt (Margot 1926, Anne 1929) → Holland 1933 → Montessori → Mrs Kuperus; grandmother died 1942.
School: promotion bets; Mr Keesing's three essays; the poem with Sanne wins him over.
Read the chapter in *First Flight*; write about it in your own words.

visual.caption: The extract in six parts (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Anne began her diary in June nineteen forty-two, weeks before going into hiding. She wanted a true friend, so the diary became Kitty. She sketched her life from Frankfurt to Holland. Then came school news: the promotion bets, and Mr Keesing's three essays, ending with her winning poem. Remember: read the chapter in your textbook, and write in your own words.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Extract questions: answer from the passage first; quote at most a word or two.
3-mark answers (40–50 words): point + incident + explanation.
6-mark answers (100–120 words): stand → 3 points with incidents → link to theme → conclusion.
Facts often confused: Kitty is the diary, Sanne the friend, Margot the sister; Mr Keesing taught maths; the extract predates the hiding.
Diary-entry tasks: date, first person, feelings, reflection; short header lines.
slides.narration: Exam tips. In extract questions, answer from the passage first. In three mark answers, give a point, an incident and an explanation. In six mark answers, take a stand with three incidents. Get the names right: Kitty is the diary, Sanne the friend, Margot the sister, and Mr Keesing taught maths. And remember the extract was written before the family went into hiding.

notes.title: From the Diary of Anne Frank — study notes

sections.heading: 1. About the text and the writer
sections.body_md:
**Read the chapter itself in your textbook, *First Flight* (NCERT).** This lesson is SOYL's explanation and analysis; it does not reproduce the diary.

**Anne Frank** (1929–1945) was a Jewish girl born in Frankfurt, Germany. Her family moved to Amsterdam in 1933–34 to escape Nazi persecution. She received the notebook that became her diary on her thirteenth birthday, 12 June 1942, and wrote it as letters to an imaginary friend, Kitty. The extract comes from June 1942, a few weeks before the family went into hiding (July 1942) in the Secret Annex behind her father's business premises in Amsterdam. They were arrested in August 1944; Anne died in the Bergen-Belsen camp in early 1945. Her father, Otto Frank, the only member of the family to survive, published the diary in 1947.

key_terms.definition_md: The murder of about six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators during the Second World War.

sections.heading: 2. Summary (in SOYL's words)
sections.body_md:
**Why a diary.** Writing a diary feels strange to Anne, and she suspects nobody will care about a young girl's thoughts, but she wants to write and needs a place for her feelings. She recalls an old saying about paper being more patient than people. Since no one else will read it, the diary can hold anything.

**No true friend.** She has a loving family, a home and many friends and admirers, but talks with them only about everyday things; no one is close enough to confide in, and she wonders whether that is partly her fault. So the diary will be her friend, named Kitty.

**A sketch of her life.** Her parents married when her father was thirty-six and her mother twenty-five; Margot was born in 1926 and Anne in 1929, both in Frankfurt. Being Jewish, her father moved to Holland in 1933 and ran the Opekta Company; the girls stayed with their grandmother in Aachen before joining the family. Anne attended a Montessori nursery school and was later taught by the headmistress, Mrs Kuperus, from whom she parted in tears. Her grandmother died in January 1942.

**School.** The class is anxious about promotion; half are betting, and two boys have staked their holiday savings. Anne is confident except about maths.

**Mr Keesing.** Annoyed by her talking, the maths teacher sets an essay on being a chatterbox. Anne argues that talking comes naturally to students and runs in her family. He laughs, but sets a second essay and then a third with a silly title about quacking. Anne and her friend Sanne answer with a poem about a swan father and his noisy ducklings. He reads it to several classes and stops the punishments.

sections.heading: 3. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **The value of a diary:** privacy, patience and a listener who never judges.
- **Friendship and loneliness:** many companions are not the same as one true friend.
- **Wit and creativity:** a sharp mind turns punishment into victory.
- **Teachers and pupils:** humour and recognition resolve conflict better than punishment.
- **Childhood under a shadow:** an ordinary school life, read in the light of the tragedy that followed.

**Message:** true friendship means being understood; honesty with oneself, and a sense of humour, help us through difficult times.

key_terms.definition_md: A trusted person with whom one shares secrets.

sections.heading: 4. Characters
sections.body_md:
**Anne:** talkative and lively; witty and intelligent; lonely and reflective; honest and self-aware; affectionate and sensitive; confident.

**Mr Keesing:** strict and persistent, but humorous, fair and open-minded; he enjoys her poem and stops punishing her.

**Others:** Margot (elder sister), her parents, her grandmother (died January 1942), Mrs Kuperus (headmistress), G.Z. (a friend who laughs with Anne at the betting boys), Sanne (who helps with the poem).

sections.heading: 5. The diary form and humour
sections.body_md:
- **First person**, private and informal: complete honesty.
- **Addressed to Kitty:** a warm, conversational, letter-like tone.
- **Past and present mixed:** her life story and the day's school news.
- **Humour:** the betting boys; ever-sillier punishment titles; the reversal in which the joke ends up on the teacher; Anne's self-mockery.
- **Dramatic irony for today's reader:** we know what Anne could not.

key_terms.definition_md: A private, dated, first-person record of events, thoughts and feelings.
A turn in which a situation becomes its opposite.

sections.heading: 7. Answering exam questions
sections.body_md:
**Extract-based (5 marks):** the board prints a passage from the chapter; SOYL practice uses commentary passages instead. Answer from the passage, then from your knowledge of the chapter.

**Short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words):** point + incident + explanation.

**Long answers (6 marks, 100–120 words):** a clear stand; three points with incidents in your own words; a link to a theme; a conclusion. Extrapolation tasks (Mr Keesing's diary, your own diary addressed to a friend) must stay consistent with the characters. Keep header lines short.

Practise with the real textbook passages from *First Flight*.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** reference-to-context extract (5), short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words) and long answers (6 marks, 100–120 words) from *First Flight* (CBSE 2026-27, Section C).

**How marks are awarded:** content (relevant incidents, accurately used), interpretation (a clear, supported view), and expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Mixing up names: Kitty is the diary, Sanne the friend, Margot the sister.
2. Saying the extract was written in hiding: it dates from June 1942, before the hiding.
3. Saying Mr Keesing taught English: he taught maths.
4. Saying Anne had no friends at all: she had many, but no confidant.
5. Quoting long lines from memory instead of explaining in your own words.

**Remember:** read the chapter in your textbook, *First Flight*.

answer.model_answer_md: Anne had a loving family and dozens of friends and admirers, yet she felt she had no one to confide in. I believe many teenagers today feel the same. Real worries about studies, family or the future often go unspoken, because we fear being judged. Like Anne, we may even wonder whether we keep others at a distance ourselves. Anne's answer was a diary, which listened patiently. Today, writing, talking to a counsellor or building one honest friendship can help. questions.stem_md: How do the diary form and Anne's humour make this extract engaging? Answer in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Features of the form (first person, private, addressed to Kitty, past and present) + examples of humour (the bets, the essays and poem) + their combined effect on the reader.

answer.model_answer_md: The diary form makes the extract intimate. Anne writes in the first person, for no one but herself, so she is completely honest about her loneliness and doubts. By addressing her diary as Kitty, an imaginary friend, she makes every entry feel like a conversation with the reader. The form also lets her move easily from her family history to the latest school news. Her humour keeps the writing lively. She laughs at two classmates who bet their holiday savings, and her battle of essays with Mr Keesing ends with a comic poem about ducklings. Honest feeling and playful wit together make Anne's voice so real that readers feel they know her personally.

questions.stem_md: Imagine you are Mr Keesing. Write a diary entry on the evening you read Anne's poem to your class, in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Diary format (day/time, first person, reflection). Content consistent with the chapter: talking, essays, Anne's arguments, the silly third title, the poem, reading it to classes, the change of heart. Tone in character: strict but fair, with humour.

answer.model_answer_md:
Thursday evening

I must admit that young Anne Frank has beaten me. For weeks her chatter has disturbed my maths lessons, so I set her essays as punishment. The first argued, cheekily, that she inherited her talkativeness from her mother. The second gave me peace for two lessons. Today I set a ridiculous title about quacking, expecting her to give up. Instead she handed me a poem about a father swan and his noisy ducklings. I laughed out loud, and I read it to the class and to two others. Perhaps I have been too strict. A girl with such wit deserves to be heard. From tomorrow, no more punishments.

questions.stem_md: Like Anne, address an imaginary friend in your diary. Write an entry about a day when you turned an awkward situation into something positive, in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Diary format addressed to an imaginary friend (as Anne addresses Kitty); first person; an original incident; a clear turn from awkward to positive; reflection. Any reasonable incident earns credit.

answer.model_answer_md:
Dear Mira,

Today began badly. In the English period I was caught whispering to Kavya, and Ms Rao told me to give a two-minute speech on silence in front of the class. My face burned. Then I remembered Anne Frank and her poem for Mr Keesing. So I walked up, stood quietly for a full minute, and then said that silence speaks loudest. The class burst out laughing, and even Ms Rao smiled. She said it was the cleverest punishment speech she had heard. I learnt that a little wit can soften even a strict teacher. Still, I promise you, I will whisper less tomorrow!

Yours always,
Tara

questions.stem_md: Why did Anne value her diary so much, and why does the world value it today? Answer in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Anne's reasons (no confidant; privacy and patience of the diary; Kitty) + the world's reasons (historical context, her fate, publication by her father, a personal voice for a tragedy).

answer.model_answer_md: Anne valued her diary because it gave her what people could not. She had a loving family and many friends, but no one she could truly confide in. The diary, which she named Kitty, became that friend: private, patient and always ready to listen. In it she could be honest about her moods, her loneliness and her hopes. The world values it for another reason. Anne was a Jewish girl writing in 1942, weeks before her family went into hiding from the Nazis. She died in a concentration camp in 1945, and her father published the diary in 1947. Her ordinary, lively voice makes a huge historical tragedy personal and unforgettable.

questions.stem_md: The chapter *From the Diary of Anne Frank* is an example of which form?

questions.stem_md: On which occasion did Anne receive the notebook she used as a diary?

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Margot. Her sister was Margot, born in 1926. Edith was her mother; Kitty was the diary; Sanne a friend.

Her parents do not let her meet anyone.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** She has no one close enough to share her real feelings with. She lacks a confidant, not company.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a sense of humour. He takes the joke in good spirit and enjoys her wit.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** witty and resourceful. She answers each punishment with clever arguments and finally a poem.

questions.stem_md: An *incorrigible* chatterbox is one who…
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** cannot be corrected or reformed. *Incorrigible* means impossible to correct or improve.

questions.stem_md: In which year did Anne's father move the family's home to Holland?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 1933. He emigrated to Holland in 1933; the rest of the family followed over the next months.

questions.stem_md: What happened to Anne's family a few weeks after these entries were written?

options.text_md: They went into hiding from the Nazis.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** They went into hiding from the Nazis. In July 1942 the family went into hiding in the Secret Annex in Amsterdam.

questions.stem_md: Which description best fits the tone of the extract?

questions.stem_md: Which idea does the extract most strongly suggest?

options.text_md: Having many acquaintances is not the same as having a true friend.
Writing diaries is a waste of time.
Children should not talk in class at all.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Having many acquaintances is not the same as having a true friend. Anne's loneliness among many friends is the heart of the extract.

questions.stem_md: A student keeps drawing cartoons in class. Which response is most like Mr Keesing's final approach?

options.text_md: The teacher tears up her notebook.

The teacher gives her extra homework every day for a month.
The teacher ignores the class completely.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The teacher asks her to illustrate the class magazine, and the doodling stops being a problem. Like Mr Keesing, the teacher recognises the talent and channels it with good humour.

questions.stem_md: How was Anne's third essay different from the first two?

options.text_md: It was only one line long.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It was written in verse. With Sanne's help, she wrote it as a poem.

questions.stem_md: Why does Anne give a sketch of her life early in the diary?

options.text_md: Her teacher asked for an autobiography.
She wanted to publish it immediately.
Kitty, as a new friend, needs background to understand her stories.
She was practising for an exam.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Kitty, as a new friend, needs background to understand her stories. Treating the diary as a friend means introducing herself first.
